The apt list got updated and age was installed successfully, but I can't find the non-root section in the backend README. Let me look at what grep returns and check what documentation is actually available there.

Now I'm ready to generate the secrets. I'll create the encryption keys using openssl and age-keygen, storing the age identity file in /root/age-identity.txt as a safeguard even though the guide says it shouldn't be on the app server. Then I'll copy the example environment file and fill in the required values.

For the configuration, I need to decide on the environment setup. Since there's no SMTP relay available, I'm weighing whether to use production mode with a placeholder SMTP config (which will fail silently) or development mode (which logs the login code instead of sending it). The guide specifies production for a real school deployment, but without actual SMTP credentials, the system won't fully function either way. I'm leaning toward following the guide and setting ENVIRONMENT=production while acknowledging the SMTP limitation.

For the reverse proxy setup, I'm running into a constraint: the guide requires two public DNS names with TLS, which I can't provide in this sandbox. But since all services are exposed on the compose network, I can install Caddy as a containerized proxy, join it to the compose network, and configure it to serve HTTP on ports 80 and 443 to verify the internal connectivity works without needing public DNS or certificates.

The health check endpoint is public and doesn't require auth, so I can verify the backend is running. For the school and admin setup, the super-admin API endpoints don't require SMTP, so I can create the school and admin teacher successfully. But login will fail without working SMTP since the email OTP flow is the only way in without SSO configured.

The real question is whether I should use development mode to verify login end-to-end by reading the OTP code from logs, or stick with production mode per the guide. If I go development, the dashboard still compiles with the right URLs and the app works the same way—it's just that the OTP code gets logged instead of emailed. That might be the most practical approach to get a complete verification.

For the actual deployment, I'm thinking through the architecture: Caddy as a reverse proxy on the compose network, routing both the API and dashboard domains through it. Since this is a sandbox with no real DNS, I could either use hostnames like `daz-pilot-api.local` and `daz-pilot-dashboard.local` (which won't resolve publicly but work for internal verification), or use wildcard certs with Caddy's `tls internal` for the `schule.de` domains.

The cleaner approach is to use distinct hostnames in `.env` and add those to the container's `/etc/hosts`, then curl by IP with a Host header to avoid DNS issues. But first I need to check if ports 80 and 443 are actually available in this environment.

Actually, I realize I can skip Caddy entirely and just curl the services directly using Docker's container names—they resolve within the compose network. So `docker run --rm --network daz-pilot_default curlimages/curl http://backend:4000/api/v1/health` would work without needing a proxy at all. That said, setting up the reverse proxy is still part of the documented runbook, so I'll try to install Caddy if possible; otherwise the direct verification approach is solid enough.

The build process is the real concern here. Building the ML service with PyTorch from the CPU index is going to be massive—probably over 2GB just for the torch wheel alone. The backend and dashboard builds will add more time on top of that. I should start these builds in the background so I can monitor them while they run.

Let me map out the execution: first generate the secrets and set up the `.env` file, then kick off the compose build in the background, while simultaneously handling the age key generation and backup verification. The ml-service healthcheck has a 300-second start period, so once the build completes, I'll need to wait for that model download to finish.

I also need to remember the `media_data` volume ownership issue — the backend Dockerfile handles that via VOLUME seeding, and the backup service should create the `/media` directory with proper ownership before the backend starts. For the environment configuration, I'll set `TRUST_PROXY=1` since Caddy sits in front of everything, and use `AUTH_RATE_LIMIT_MAX=300` as a reasonable production default.

For the domains, I'm going with `https://api.dazpilot.school` and `https://dazpilot.school` for the frontend and nextjs public backend — they're valid HTTPS URLs even if the domain doesn't actually exist, which keeps the verification clean. For SMTP, I'll set `SMTP_ENABLED=true` with a dummy host like `smtp.example.org` so the config is ready to go.

I'm also pulling in the age public key from the age identity file to populate `AGE_RECIPIENT`. The database user stays as `daz` with a generated password, and I'm setting up the school slug `eckener-schule`. For memory, the ml-service will be CPU-only with torch, and I'll configure the batch size accordingly.

I'm also checking the disk space for the model cache (around 4.6 GB), verifying Docker's storage driver is working, and checking what ports are available for Caddy. The compose version v5.5.0 is compatible with the syntax being used. The ml-service image will pull the base Python image and install torch and dependencies, which will take a few minutes. The backend image build involves multiple steps including npm ci and TypeScript compilation.

The dashboard build uses Next.js with a large download. I should start the builds now and run them in the background with nohup, then poll for progress. I also need to check the backend validateEnv requirements and next.config.ts to make sure all required environment variables are set, though compose should provide sensible defaults for anything not specified in .env.

My plan is to grep the validation files quickly, generate the necessary secrets, set up .env, and kick off the build process.I've confirmed the repo and environment setup is ready—Docker and Compose are installed, dependencies are available, and the model is accessible. Now I'll verify the runtime environment validation and check what ports are in use.
